transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Daniel Park (Redwood SE); James Liu (CTO, Aperture Systems); Priya Nair (SRE Lead); Carlos Mendes (Head of ML)

Summary:
- Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for latency-sensitive payment auth flows and chat assistant.
- Main concerns: multi-region failover, SLA commitments, model fallbacks when capacity or region fails, and security/compliance for PII.
- Agreed next steps: send security docs, plan pilot on Dedicated with canary fallbacks, schedule benchmark.

Transcript:
00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining - can you hear me okay? ... cool. We'll do quick intros and then Daniel will dig into the multi-region questions you sent over.
00:17 James (Aperture): Yep, all good. James here, CTO. Our main thing is payment auth latency, p99 needs to be under 150ms for our EU region, ideally with failover to US if EU has issues.
00:32 Maya: Great, that's helpful. Priya, from SRE side, do you want to add constraints? 
00:38 Priya: Sure, we run across two regions, eu-west and us-east, and we need both active-active. We also need audit logs and KMS integration for keys. One big ask: in failover we cannot see >2x p99 increase or we risk timeouts in our stack.
00:56 Daniel (Redwood SE): Right, understood. A couple clarifications - when you say failover do you mean automatic routing at the edge to US if eu-west is degraded, or prefer a client-side retry? Both are possible but tradeoffs.
01:11 Carlos (ML): We also have a smaller conversational model for low-latency auth prompts, and a larger model for long form support. We might want automatic fallback to a lighter model during incidents.
01:25 Daniel: Yep, that's a common pattern - our routing policies can be latency-first or cost-first, and we support model variant fallback. In hosted mode we provide managed multi-region endpoints with active-active routing and automatic failover policies.
01:41 James: What does automatic failover look like? Worst-case, if eu-west loses a couple machines, how quickly would traffic shift and do you preserve KV cache? We rely on prefix caching to avoid warm-start latencies.
01:59 Daniel: Good question - in Dedicated we run your reserved pool in specific regions; you can opt for geo-redundant pods. Failover is handled by our routing layer, typically within 10-30s for DNS + healthchecks, but for lower RTO we recommend cross-region replication of prefix/KV caches - we can replicate keys async, but there is a small window of cold-start.
02:21 Priya: 10-30 seconds is okay but our payment stack has 3s timeout. So we need an intermediate strategy - local call to local cache, and fallback to a small model in the same region if the heavy model isn't warm.
02:35 Daniel: That's reasonable: we support hierarchical fallbacks - first try same-region hot cache, then lightweight local model (quantized), then cross-region call. That keeps p99 from spiking too high.
02:47 Maya: Also worth noting we support canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies - if a new model causes higher latency or error rates, the routing can automatically revert.
03:00 Carlos: How about SLA terms? For Dedicated customers do you offer latency SLOs or just uptime? We need something enforceable in contract for p99 latency.
03:09 Maya: Our standard SLA focuses on availability and uptime for Dedicated. Latency SLOs are available in enterprise contracts - we can include p99 latency targets and credits. We'll need to see traffic profile to put realistic numbers.
03:22 James: Ok, send contract examples. Also need SOC2 and encryption at rest details.
03:29 Maya: Absolutely - we'll send the security packet. Daniel, can you walk through a sample architecture diagram for the failover sequence? 
03:35 Daniel: Sure. (Speaker 1) I'll share screen... so imagine eu-west and us-east pods, load balancer with healthchecks, local KV cache in each region, prefix replication to us-east, and a lightweight quantized model pinned locally for emergency fallback. The order is: local model -> cross-region -> degrade to smaller model, and if all else fails return cached response or graceful error.
04:06 Priya: Any spec on consistency when replicating KV cache? We can't tolerate inconsistent auth decisions.
04:11 Daniel: For auth flows we recommend synchronous replication for critical keys - we can do synchronous writes with fallback to read-only mode during partitions; that avoids split-brain for auth decisions.
04:23 Carlos: For model fallback, how do you guarantee output quality? If we fallback to smaller model for auth classification, risk of higher false positives.
04:32 Daniel: We run quality monitors and can tie regressions to eval prompts; during pilot we'll validate the fallback model against your golden set. Also you can configure scoring thresholds to require second-step verification.
04:45 James: If we go Hosted instead of Dedicated, how much control do we lose over failover behavior? 
04:50 Maya: Hosted is the fastest to adopt but it's our managed multi-tenant infra - you get geo routing and fallbacks but less isolation. Dedicated gives reserved capacity + more control over replication and can have stricter SLAs and isolation; Private gives the most control (VPC) but slower onboarding and more ops.
05:09 Priya: Does Private support on-prem with HSM for KMS? We need HSM for keys for EU data residency.
05:15 Daniel: Yes, Private can be deployed into your VPC or on-prem with HSM integration. That option includes full audit logs and we can map to your KMS/HSM for FIPS 140-2.
05:26 James: Great. What's the typical timeline to stand up a Dedicated pilot with multi-region? 
05:30 Maya: For a dedicated pilot it's usually 2-4 weeks depending on networking and infra approvals; Private on-prem might be 6-8 weeks.
05:39 Carlos: For the pilot, can we benchmark tail latency p99 across eu-west/us-east with our real traffic? 
05:44 Daniel: Yes we'll run a benchmarking session; we'll want a representative traffic replay and will measure p50/p95/p99, cold/warm cache, and failover RTO.
05:55 Priya: Another question on billing - if we have cross-region failover that uses US capacity does that incur extra cost? 
06:01 Maya: Yes, cross-region usage will count against the region's capacity; for Dedicated you can reserve capacity in both regions or opt for burst to other regions at premium rates.
06:11 James: Any competitors we should compare to? We looked at OpenAI and Bedrock, but they don't offer Dedicated pools with that level of replication control out of the box. Seldon is more DIY.
06:25 Maya: Right, we often position Redwood for teams who want control over serving economics and predictable latency.
06:31 Carlos: Ok, let's talk about the pilot scope - we want: (1) validate p99 <150ms EU with fallback, (2) test failover RTO under instance loss, (3) verify KMS/HSM flow, (4) measure cost delta when failover to US.
06:45 Daniel: We'll put together a pilot plan with test cases for each of those bullets. Quick note - for p99 <150ms we may recommend smaller model in-region + e2e optimizations like request coalescing and prefix caching.
06:58 Priya: Can you also include logging level for audit trails? We need per-request trace IDs and token-level cost breakdowns. 
07:06 Daniel: Yep, Redwood Console exposes tracing and token-level cost; we can add retention options for logs and integrate with your SIEM.
07:15 James: Next steps then?
07:17 Maya: Action items: we'll send SOC2/security packet and SOW, Daniel will draft benchmarking plan, Priya will share traffic patterns. We'll reconvene after docs and plan are shared.
07:28 Priya: Sounds good.
07:29 Carlos: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
